title: Points, stamps, and what they are really worth
description: Loyalty points feel like a bonus, but they are a currency with an exchange rate set by the shop. Do the conversion before you chase them.

body.heading: Find the exchange rate
paragraphs: Points are worth whatever they buy. If 100 points earn you $1 off, each point is worth one cent, and earning one point per dollar means the scheme returns about 1% of your spending — eventually, and only at that shop.
That is not nothing, but it reframes the chase: spending an extra $20 to "earn" points returns roughly 20 cents of value. Points should reward shopping you were doing anyway, never direct it.

body.heading: The traps in the small print
paragraphs: Points often expire, can be devalued when the shop changes the conversion rate, and sometimes require a minimum spend to unlock. A balance you never quite reach is a loan of your loyalty at zero interest — to the shop.
Double-points events deserve the same maths as sales: the discount is the points' real value, not the glittering headline number of points themselves.

body.heading: Use schemes passively
paragraphs: The healthy relationship with loyalty schemes is passive: carry the card for shops you already use, collect what falls your way, and spend points on things you would have bought. The moment a scheme changes where you shop or what you buy, it is working for the shop, not for you.

One exception is worth making: points and stamps that are about to expire. Spending a nearly expired balance on something genuinely useful is recovering your own money. Set a reminder rather than letting the balance evaporate.

takeaway: Convert points to money before valuing them — usually about a cent each — and let schemes reward your normal shopping rather than steer it.
